utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in court today. Mr. Registrar, may you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to our colleagues from the OTP and to all in the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson as Defence for General Delic, with the assistance of Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Your apologies. We just have a small technical problem here at the Bench, if the parties will excuse us for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Alastair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Duncan, can you please give us your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: 22nd of October, 1952, Toft Monks in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Duncan, where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm currently employed as the managing director of the services Sound and Vision Corporation, which deploys television and radio to those British soldiers deployed around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, prior to joining the Sound and Vision Corporation, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I was 34 years in Her Majesty's Armed Forces, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time you left the British Army, what rank did you hold and in what position were you serving?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'd been -- I was a major general, and I'd been running the British Army's Warfare Centre in Warminster with responsibility for the training and deployment of all British soldiers on operations in the last two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you prefer to be referred to as "Mr. Duncan or "Major General Duncan"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you could very briefly give the Trial Chamber a run down of your military career from the time you joined Her Majesty's Armed Forces until the time you retired as a major general.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Thank you. I joined the British Army in 1970 and went to Sandhurst for two years, and then after that went through a number of appointments in the infantry with my own battalion and also in instructional posts outside my battalion. I then went to Staff College. I went to the High Command Staff Court and the Royal College of Defence Studies, and after that I did a number of promotional jobs command commanding my battalion in 1993 in Bosnia, later on commanding the Bosnian Zone from Banja Luka, and later beyond that as a brigadier 19 Brigade deployed again on operations. In the meantime, a number of trips to Northern Ireland, and then finally my two year stint, which I thoroughly enjoyed, training the British Army. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to "my battalion," which battalion were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I refer to the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire, which is a single-battalion regiment composed of about 600 people, a body of infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is it [indiscernible] for the Prince of Wales?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't really got any association for the Prince of Wales, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, of the 34 years you spent in Her Majesty's Armed Forces, how long were you a member of the 1st Prince of Wales Own Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: For the first four years, and then in Northern Ireland for a further two years, and then was in and out, really, three years on employment with the Staff, and then you come back to your regiment. So you hop in and out of your regiment when you move up through the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the most senior position you held within the 1st Prince of Wales' Own Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: As the commanding officer for a period of three years from 1990 to 1993, an unusually long time for a commanding officer, where commanding officers normally have about two years. I managed to squeeze three, which was quite useful for me, but it also meant that the soldiers who worked for me understood how we thought and what we did, and more particularly how I thought, and what I did. And we had been on operations in Belfast in 1990 as a team, so we were a proven team, as it were, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, just for the sake of -- or perhaps to save my own voice, I will be referring to your battalion as "1PWO." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's actually an acronym that was used within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when 1PWO was deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. We had a message late in 1992 that we would take over from the 1st Battalion, the Cheshire Regiment, that was already in Herzegovina and Bosnia, and we therefore started training for that task. And I knew that we were going there, so I did two reconnaissances before Christmas to see what was there, because clearly I needed to go on the ground and see what the situation was like in order to be able to adjust the organisation of my battalion best able to do its task in theatre. I did two of those reconnaissances, and finally we deployed on the -- I deployed on the 11th of April, and we took over -- I apologise. We deployed on the 5th of April, and we took over the task on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you mentioned relieving the Cheshire regiment. Do you know who was the commanding officer of the Cheshire regiment at the time 1PWO relieved that regiment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, it was Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart from the Cheshire regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the sake of completeness, how long was 1PWO deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this tour?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It was deployed from the 11th of April to the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Trial Chamber under what authority or under what type of structure your battalion was deployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We were deployed as part of the United Nations force which had been authorised and deployed to provide aid to the stricken people there, directly deployed under the headquarters in Kiseljak, the High Command there, which was a military headquarters, and the political headquarters which was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did this United Nations force that you're referring to go by any acronym or abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the military headquarters in Kiseljak, did that have a particular name or acronym that it was known as?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It had a number of names which we called it from time to time. I can't particularly remember. It was just known as our high formation headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could assist, was it also known as BH Command?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what the mission of UNPROFOR and, more particularly, 1PWO, during the course of its deployment in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Certainly. The mission was to provide aid and make sure the aid was delivered to whoever required it, both in my area of interest and those other areas that needed it, so we were to help the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees deploy aid to those people who required it in that theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us, during the time period that your battalion was deployed, to whom you reported?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I reported to the headquarters at Kiseljak that you just referred to, but I also reported to Robin Searby, who is a brigadier, who is based in Split on the coast of Croatia, who was my British commanding officer, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record, sir, could you tell us who was in command at BH Command during this time period in 1993, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't recall, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And for the sake, sir, of completeness, when your battalion left Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the end of 1993, were you relieved by any other unit?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We were relieved by the 1st Battalion, the Coldstream Guards, which was commanded by a Lieutenant-Colonel, Peter Phillips -- Peter Williams, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Also from Britain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also from Britain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, during the time period that your battalion was deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, about the structure of your battalion, and how you organised it in order to fulfill its mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. It was very unusual. The ground that was given to me to cover started at Romboci, went north from there to Gornji Vakuf, north from there to Novi Travnik, then east to Vitez, and then north from there right the way up to Zenica, and then on from Zenica to Tuzla in the north, a distance of 180 kilometres, which for a British battalion was a very unusual number of ground to cover. However, I decided that we needed a strong presence in Tuzla, so I kept a company of my troops up there, the majority of my people in Vitez, in the centre, and a fourth company at Gornji Vakuf. I was then able to cover much of that 180 kilometres and to also make sure I could fill my task, which was making sure that guaranteed to get the aid to where it was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, how your unit was structured in terms of the people who actually went out and were on the ground and covering that area that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Certainly. One of the most important things about my operation was making sure I knew what was going on in my area of responsibility, and so we had a series of layers of information-gathering. The first layer was those soldiers who were deployed in armoured vehicles or also in Land Rovers, would be going out and talking to the local people and to the local soldiers and gathering information of what was going on in the area. And that was the sort of blanket underneath the first level. The second level was a bunch of seven or eight very experienced captains in my unit, who I'd known very well, and they went out specifically to cover areas of interest within our area so that we could talk to the brigades that were going on, and the battalions that were going and see what they -- so that was a level above. And above that we had company commanders who were in charge of groups of about 100 people, and I sent them out separately to reach out to the brigade commanders. So we had three layers, and on top of that was myself, and I would speak to the corps commanders in particular. The reason for making sure we had those five layers is to make sure that we didn't cross over with the information, and the plan from that was everything was then drawn in every day, and we could then find out what was going on, which routes were open, which routes were closed, where there were problems, where we got information in that things needed to be done, and that is how we worked throughout the time we were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, some follow-up questions based on what you've just told us. First of all, these small groups of soldiers deployed in armoured vehicles, did they go by any particular terms?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The armoured vehicles were two types. One was a Warrior armoured vehicle, that was the nomenclature, that had a crew in the back of about six people and a cannon on top, which is 30-millimetres, and they would normally go out in pairs. This is -- that is quite a powerful force and we would deploy with care. We also had a vehicle called a 432. That was similar to the Warrior except it didn't have a cannon on top at all, and that could do similar tasks. And then finally we would go to vehicles, which had no armament at all, which were issued to my liaison officers, because we felt they had a much less aggressive role because they were just Land Rovers, and they could get amongst people and talk with ease with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these Warriors and the 432 vehicles, were they tracked or wheeled armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The Warrior and the 432 were both tracked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about reporting procedures in your battalion during the time you commanded while in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us about reporting procedures and how you went about reporting information?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. Hopefully I've just outlined the five layers that we have of reporting back, but the important thing with that is that every evening at 6.00, all that information which had been gathered during the day had been put together by Simon Harrison, who was my intelligence officer, and I say "intelligence officer" because that's what he was doing. He was gathering that information, so we had a complete picture, probably the best picture of -- that anyone had at that time, of the whole of the area. That picture was then given back to everybody at the 6.00 meeting to make sure that it was correct and people could -- who went to that meeting at 6.00 were not only my own soldiers, they were UNHCR people, they were Red Cross people, ECMM people, everybody who was involved in trying to get that aid through to people came to that meeting. And having done the meeting and adjusted, we then produced a thing called a Military Information Sum, which was sent out to everybody in my organisation, also downwards, upwards and sideways, so that everybody knew the situation that was going on, and they could see that and adjust their patrols and conduct the next day. And that was a process that went on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll see a few of these military information sums or milinfosums in a few moments, but can you just tell us a little bit about how those documents were structured and what were -- the way those documents were presented, and what was done with those documents once they were finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, may I interrupt, because before we go into that, I would like to ask you, General: Who was above and to the sides of the flow of information that you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To one side we had the Canadian Battalion, who were in Visoko, and we also had a French Battalion, they were in Kakanj up the road. But apart from that, it was very open, indeed, because we had this huge distance to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And above?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Above was the headquarters in Kiseljak, the BHC command, and we reported to them every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any of this information was made available somehow to the warring parties in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would not be normally made to the warring parties at all, no. That was -- this information we were gathering was so that we had a picture, the armed forces had a picture, the UNHCR had a picture, and all those agencies had a good picture, so we could work together. It was really to make sure that we had unity of effort to what we were trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right, but I suppose that just as interesting it was for you to find out what they were doing, it would be equally interesting for them to find out what you knew, and that is why I was asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were obviously -- I think, sir, they would obviously keep tabs on what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To follow up on a question that Judge Harhoff has just asked, you told us, sir, about your battalion having liaison officers to the parties. Were there any other liaison officers going the other direction?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It was -- I managed to persuade the warring parties to send liaison officers back to me. This was a fairly risky affair, but it was worth doing because it gained our confidence, particularly with the commanders. Those liaison officers would be expected to talk to brigade-level commanders in the same way that my people were talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General, which parties had liaison officers to 1PWO during this time period you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It was done regionally, so we moved across the various regions, and we moved those deployments as the -- my apologies. We moved those deployments as those deployments changed from time to time. It was about ten officers altogether which moved around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What kind of information was exchanged between these liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between liaison officers, we would tell them what we were doing, we would tell them where the aid convoys were going so that we could hopefully preempt any problems with the aid, particularly. And then we would hopefully find out what they were doing so that they wouldn't be doing anything that stopped us going. So a two-way system, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did they tell you what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Duncan, let me go back to the milinfosums. Can you tell us a little bit about how those documents were structured and what was done with those documents once they were completed and had been vetted internally?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The first thing is that all this information which came in to my captain, Captain Harrison, in the headquarters was collated together to make sure it made sense, and we didn't overlap, and we didn't double-report what was going on and things like that. So we made sure we had a, for the 6.00 meeting, a good information. That was then discussed at the 6.00 meeting to make sure that everybody was happy with it, and from there we produced a milinfosum which essentially was the facts with a header on top, and underneath it, normally by locations, what was going on in each location for that particular day, and finishing up at the end sometimes with a conclusion, a suggestion, and things like that, for the next day and -- and I would sign that off every day, either myself personally or my second in command would sign that off to make sure that we had got the right information, and we were doing things correctly for the next day. I should add that one of the major points I made as commanding officer there was for the soldiers on the ground to think if what they did was going to help to get the aid through, that was good and they should do it. But if they felt it was not going to get the aid through, they shouldn't do it, because you can imagine with a force which was deployed over 180 kilometres, I can't micromanage what they're doing, and they need to do have an idea, clearly they needed to know how to get the aid through, but also at the same time, will this help my commanding officer or will this hinder and that was a guideline which was very useful for everybody across. I digressed a little bit, which I apologise, Your Honours, but that's how it was put together every day. That information sum was then passed sideways to everybody downwards to my units and also upwards. So that again, everybody involved, including ECMM, UNHCR knew what was going on. It was a team effort every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, when you indicate in that answer that you would sign off on the document, did you physically sign the documents, did you write your name on the documents, or what do you mean you say you would sign off on it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would then tell the captain, "That's it, put it, send it off now," and it would go off in the form of a fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My signature is indecipherable, sir, so it didn't matter. Going off as a fax meant that it had been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A signature doesn't have to be deciphered, it just has to be recognised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was scratched, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Recognised as your sign.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did put a signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did put my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Duncan, let me ask you, sir, about the situation in Central Bosnia in 1993 at the time your unit arrived there, in terms of the overall strategic situation in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Before I'd arrived there, rather, it was relatively benign on the two reconnaissances that I'd done. But when I got there for my deployment on the 5th, we were then immediately involved in Ahmici and the problem there, which was basically that the Muslims living there had been slaughtered by the HVO or their troops and had knocked people out, and clearly the atmosphere was pretty awful in that stage. A huge atrocity had been done, and within days I found myself in Ahmici finding the bodies and helping to clear up which was a most terrible situation, a situation which was rapidly picked up by the press and transmitted around the world as a terrible atrocity. As a result of that atrocity, the HVO forces, the Croat forces, and the BiH forces, mainly the Muslim forces, fell out with one another completely, and this terrible period of a fight or a war within a war started in Bosnia. So instead of taking their effort to try and prevent the Serb forces coming in, which they had been doing, we now had this internecine battle inside Bosnia which was doing us no good, them no good, and no good at all. And it meant now we had much more difficulties in getting the aid through, as the situation had collapsed very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the ARBiH and the HVO forces, can you give us a picture of the tactical situation in terms of various advantages and strength and weaknesses of those two parties in the early part of the tour of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: In round terms the BiH, ABiH, had an awful lot of soldiers, but not a lot of equipment. And the HVO forces had a lot of equipment but a limited number of people, so you had a dichotomy between the two. It meant that it was quite difficult for people to sustain a battle, and therefore when an advance was taken, it tended to peter out very quickly, and also the lie of the land in that Lasva Valley had a road running all the way through it, like a spine; and therefore, the HVO forces, who had few numbers, could quickly deploy along that spine like a fire brigade to block off any attacks. So we were surrounded, or had begun to be surrounded, in an area which was controlled outside by the BiH forces and inside by HVO. That didn't happen overnight, it's a situation that developed, and it developed because both sides began, if you like, ethnic cleansing, moving forward in areas which they believed, rightly or wrongly, were for themselves, and moving people out, setting fire to their houses, and killing them, and a number of atrocities which again we tried to stop as best we could. It was an unpleasant place to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, you told us earlier that your -- one of your primary tasks was dealing with the senior leaders of the parties. Can you tell us with whom you dealt, starting on the ARBiH side?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: On the ARBiH side, I spoke to Enver Hadzihasanovic and Jamie Merdan, who was his 2 IC, and I spent a lot of time talking to him because he was the commander of the 3rd Corps based in Zenica. So I would drive across perhaps two or three times a week and go and see him, talk through the problems that we had, mutual problems, and to see whether we could do anything about it. In a similar manner, I would go see Tihomir Blaskic, who was commanding the HVO forces in the centre, who was based in Vitez, and I would drive across with him. And I was a bit of a messenger boy at that time, trying to coordinate the two and get them together. And that's what we did. We got them together into a joint mission with the Red Cross and everybody else involved to try and thrash out the problems and to prevent them happening. It worked quite well, but I'm afraid after a bit you get to a stage where it's quite clear that whatever you do, both sides were at each other's throats, and therefore we were unable to get any further. But certainly despite that, I carried on keeping that relationship with the two, if you like, major commanders in the area, one ABiH and one Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about Enver Hadzihasanovic. What position did he hold at the time you were meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how frequently or how often you would have met with General Hadzihasanovic during this time period of your deployment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It depended on events, because sometimes we couldn't get through, but two or three times a week, if I could make it. And I would also go and see it clearly. If he sent me a message, "can we talk."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, sir, were some of the topics that you would have discussed with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We discussed the routes through the area, because clearly when sides -- warring sides are at each other's throats, it's difficult to cross those sort of front lines. We discussed that the right amount of food was going to people, and that's one of the tasks of my liaison officers, to make sure that the food had been distributed round the place in the correct manner, and we discussed other matters as they came up, including fishing and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than fishing and other things, do you recall any of the specific other matters or problems that you addressed with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: They tended to be addressed as and when they came. There wasn't any sort of agenda that came in whenever we met. It was normally generated by a problem or something that needed to be resolved or a question from the senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with an entity that was known as the "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I am. The joint command was initially -- there was two joint commands. There was a joint command in Travnik. Are you referring to that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with that one.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. There was a joint command in Travnik, because prior to my arrival, the HVO and the BiH were fighting against the VRS, that's the Serbs, in the west and keeping them out from Travnik. In order to do that, they had agreed to get together, and they had a joint command in Travnik and that was going extremely well. However, after Ahmici and other atrocities, it tended to fall apart. So that joint command was fairly short-lived after the time I'd got there, but unfortunately it didn't work very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the other joint command?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The other joint command was an initiative by myself to get together the senior commanders from BiH and from HVO as often as possible, perhaps once a week, with their teams, so that we could thrash through all the problems and try and stop all these atrocities and animosities and fighting going on because it wasn't helping their effort or us. And therefore I wanted to get them together and discuss such things as prisoner exchange, the exchange of bodies, the routes that we could use through and beyond as it came through, and other things like that. It was to unstick the problems we had in the area. It worked reasonably well until both sides didn't want it to work, and then we had to stop, because there was no trying -- trying to force. You can take the horse to water, but it might not want to drink it and that's the stage we got to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We need to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, and also, sir, if you can pause between my question and giving an answer so the interpreters can stay with us, please.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that the -- and I'm referring now to this second joint command, not the Travnik Joint Command. This second joint command, you told us that it was an initiative to get together the senior commanders from BiH and from HVO. Do you recall which senior commanders would attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. It would be Hadzihasanovic and Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now turn, sir, to a different topic, and I would ask you if you have any information or any knowledge about the system of command and control within the 3rd Corps, based upon what you observed or based upon meetings you held with senior members of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: As a result of my talks to the senior commanders, and also the system we had set up across the area that we had, we had an extremely good plan, if you like, of what was going on for both the HVO and the ABiH. That plan was transformed into a -- on a piece of paper, one piece of paper, which quite simply had the corps headquarters at the top, and which were the subsidiary brigade headquarters under that, and then broken down all the way down to battalion level. So we could plot where those forces were for both sides. So in terms of knowing what was going on, we had a living document that was changed very often at the evening conference to move things around a bit to see where they were, and we had that document which we ran all the way through to enable us to see what was going on. So we knew what was going on right the way across.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, can you tell us if you were aware of any communication systems that the 3rd Corps Command had?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Command had initially access to telephones through the telephone exchange in Vitez, but after Ahmici that facility was, not surprisingly, unplugged. But besides that, they had satellite telephones, and I knew that because they had given me the phone numbers in case we wanted to call. And on top of that, I knew they had very clear communications back to Sarajevo. That was very useful as well.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, I'd like to ask you a follow-up based on what you've told us. In your answer as reflected on lines 11 and 12, you said: "I knew they had very clear communications back to Sarajevo." And my question to you, sir, is: What is the basis for that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The basis for that statement is, because when I asked questions about what was going on in Sarajevo or in other areas, I could get a quick, a very -- a quick message back. Or if they wanted me to talk about something, we could do that as well. I just felt that you could get an answer very quickly from 3rd Corps, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now turn, sir, to the events in June of 1993 or to focus your mind on June 1993. Can you tell us what the situation was like in Central Bosnia in the first few days of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm afraid with the passage of time, the dates are quite difficult to know what's going on. If you were to tell me there was some activity happening, but I really can't pick out a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if you recall whether you had any meetings in the first few days of June 1993 with Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, almost certainly I would have had meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document marked PT01163. That's PT01163.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Duncan, since this is the first time we're looking at one of these documents, can you tell the Trial Chamber what is appearing on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The top line is referring to what it is, in that case 1PWO, which we've already discussed, is nomenclature of my battalion. The "No info sum" is short of where putting the military information sum, the number"037," merely gives it its sequence, and dated the 15th of June, 1993, would be the day that I signed it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it be the 15th or the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you're absolutely right, the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you this, sir, in light of what you've just told us in terms about the date that you signed it off. Do you see your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could scroll down to the bottom of this page. Could we go to the bottom of the page, please? Can we go to the second page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see your signature on any of these pages?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Not at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then ask you, have you had the opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you focus your attention, please, on the fifth paragraph of this document, paragraph 5, under the heading "Zenica."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what is being reported in this paragraph of the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: This paragraph 5 refers to my meeting with Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of 3 Corps, to discuss the problem of Travnik, and it says -- and this is essentially my recall, both from my mind and from my staff officer that came with me, the detail of our meeting and what we had discussed. And that runs through that document right the way down as far as the word, which is in bold, "Comment." All that above, from "Zenica" down to the word "Comment," will be the actual fact, and the comment itself would be an expression of what we thought was going to happen. So the first bit is fact, the second bit is comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, just for the benefit of everyone present, so that we all understand, the first line of paragraph 5, if you will, there's a -- it's indicated "CO 1-PWO." Can you tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That refers directly to me as the commanding officer of the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire, i.e., 1PWO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness now be shown PT01171, PT01171.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While this document is coming up, General Duncan, let me ask you a little bit more about these comments that appear in some of these documents. Can you tell us a little bit about how the comment came to be created and what the purpose of the comment was or comments are?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The comments are generally formed by my intelligence officer as a result of what has been happening over a period of time, in terms of incidents, or trends, or ideas of what might happen in the future. He would put those down as guidance for people as to what might then happen in the future. It's merely his thoughts. It is not taken as gospel truth. The bit above will be pretty well 100 per cent correct. It's merely the comment is there to give some guidance to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, what was the -- how would the intelligence officer be in a position to make these type of comments?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: His -- my intelligence officer's entire life was sitting in his office, gathering in the information that was coming in from everybody and pulling that all together and that's what he did every single day, unless his second in command stepped in because he had to go somewhere, but that was pulled together. He therefore lived the organisations. He was, if you like, a living computer in those days, in 1993. He knew what was going on everywhere, it was in his head. He could recall things, and he was my intelligence officer because, I have to say, he was an extremely bright officer in my regiment, and he would put those milinfosums together and put the comments together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any occasion where you, as the commanding officer, disagreed with any of those comments?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions I did disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what would be the result if you disagreed with a comment, a proposed comment or a comment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would then not sign off straightaway. We'd discuss why his comment -- I wasn't happy with it, and if necessary we would change the comment. But very often, because he in many ways had a much closer idea of what was going on, he could justify his comments. So it was a discussion between myself and him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the comments that are reflected in the written documents, did you ever have any disagreements with anything that went out in the written milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Again, yes, on many occasions. I say "on many occasions" because this report was produced every day, and therefore we produced a lot of reports. But clearly if I'd come back late and wanted to change something and put it in, it could be fed in at the last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's now look at the document in front of you, sir, and can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. That is again 1PWO, my battle group's milinfosum 038, dated the 6th of June, 1993, which reports from Tuzla in this case, where we had a force up there, a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we now please go in the English version to page 5 and in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave -- could we just get back to the page we just left, because, General, I'd like you just to explain to us what the references are under Heading D: "BSA Equipment Locations," and then you mention Howitzer and tanks and mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then a number of things, are they grid references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's horribly hieroglyphical, and I apologise, it's military. In short it refers to the types - you're exactly right, sir - it refers to types of vehicles, in this case, and 120-millimetre 155 Howitzers, and those lists - you're absolutely correct, sir - that is a list of the grids where they were seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So my question is: Did the force that was observed here have one Howitzer that was seen at, one, two, three, four, five, six locations that day, or does it mean that there were six Howitzers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means there were six Howitzers, sir, one at these -- those Howitzers were at those grid points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if you look down under "Three tanks," did they have that many tanks? Apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I -- sir, can I just remind you that those are Bosnian Serb army tanks and not HVO or ABiH, so these will be observed over the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm just surprised because I thought you told us a while ago that the ABiH was under-equipped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, sir. These are Serbian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. These are Serbian vehicles, these ones. They're from the BSA, "BSA" being Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes, I misheard that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General Duncan, because we'll also see this abbreviation commonly in a number of the milinfosums, can you tell us what the abbreviation "C\S" is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, "C\S" is an abbreviation for call sign. It will appear quite often on milinfosums; although, it may not be on this milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you excuse my slowness on the uptake, was "C\S" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "C\S" does not appear on this page. I'm simply asking him because, we will see that on a number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to ask about what I see on this document. Now, will you excuse me, I know absolutely nothing about the military, so I see Judge Harhoff here knows that"CQ" means a grid. What about grid? What's a grid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A grid is a location, merely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Some specified area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- on our maps, we have a grid on the map, and within that you get 100 spaces, as it were, and you can therefore give it a nomenclature. So by running 305179, it gives you -- to walk across and down, it gives you a spot which is exactly accurate as to what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is "Sqn," "Squadron"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's squadron, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is "B" before "Squadron"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "BSA" are you talking to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just under the heading "Tuzla," number 1, "B Squadron"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: B Squadron, yes, yes. Those were the -- that's the name of the squadron that was deployed up in Tuzla, the grouping, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for the British Army's numenclature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem. You didn't write this with a view to coming to testify. It was for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return, General Duncan, to the "C\S." You told us that that referred to -- can you please tell us again?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It refers directly to a call sign. The call sign will be normally the radio sign of that vehicle, so it will be known by a call sign. It will probably have it painted on the back door and the sides as well, so you could see that is call sign so-and-so, what type of vehicle it was, and you know what it is because you've heard it speak over the air. It enables us to track what's going on. It's merely call sign X or Y will come in and put their reports in it, it just gets for our milinfosum, it tells us who said it, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is a sign on one of your vehicles or one of the army vehicles that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are Bosnian Serb Army equipment, so they will not be on our -- yes. If I just turn to -- if I may for a moment, sir, to point C on that, it says: "50 times Bosnian Serb Army tanks," so that's why we've got the numbers there, which are quite large. They're not Croat or ABiH at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 5 in the English version and page 6 in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you look at paragraph 10 as a starting point. Can you tell us what paragraph 10 is referring to, what it's relating to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 relates to two meetings, first chaired by Ambassador Thebault, who was with the European Commission Monitoring Force, and the second by myself, in an attempt to effect a ceasefire. And we pulled together those list of commanders, senior commanders, from both HVO and ABiH. Those got together for that meeting, and I chaired it with Thebault, and it was an attempt to get people together as a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can we look now at paragraph 11, and simply for the benefit of the Chamber, if you look at paragraph 11, sir, and in the middle of that paragraph you see a comment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to tie up to a question I asked a few moments ago, can you tell us what that comment means?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The Comment in that case means that the following information or the following sentences, until comment ends, is the perception of my intelligence officer, and it says that call signs have reported large numbers of Croats ready to leave the town, and are claiming they wished to move to Novi Bila. Now, that is his comment of what's happening. It's not particularly fact, but it's what might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I would turn your attention, sir, to paragraph 12, and if you could take a quick look at that to perhaps refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I do recall that. We were due to reconvene at 1800 hours that evening, but without the planned attendance of either Blaskic, the senior HVO, and Hadzihasanovic, it really didn't get very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 284.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, I'd now like to turn to or focus your attention on, again, the first half of June 1993. Did there come a time, sir, where active fighting erupted in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Fighting erupted in Central Bosnia, particularly around the area of the Lasva Valley, in a sporadic way. It was -- it is difficult to point out individual activities, although sometimes we could, from our milinfosums, discover what was likely to happen and put that down. It is -- was an attempt much of the time for the ABiH to try to cut that spinal road through, which was an essential thing for them to do and that is really -- that dominates the area at that time, their attempts to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if you recall, when this fighting erupted, the date?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't. I haven't got the dates at my fingertip after these years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness could be shown the document marked PT01189. That's PT01189.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, again for the record, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Again, it's a milinfosum generated by my battalion, number 40, dated the 8th of June, 1993. It starts with "Vitez," where clearly there were some rounds -- single rounds fired from rifles, I suspect, but not really significant. Of more significant is the second paragraph there, where it says "General," and it explains or, rather, describes that the expected BiH offensive in the area has begun, and then it recounts the detail of the advance forward by reference to various villages which had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And does this milinfosum relate to the combat operations you were just describing a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Very much so, yes. Absolutely. This describes in some detail what has happened, and again it is a result of gathering of information over a period of time, and perhaps on a short period of time when everything erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, I would just ask -- I'm going to show you another document, but I would ask you if you could again take a look at the number of this milinfosum and the date of it, and keep that in mind as we look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown PT01209. That's PT --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that this be admitted, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, PT01209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Registrar, did you say Exhibit 285?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, 285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the transcript says "289". May the record show it's 285 and not 289. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Duncan, do you see the document that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Again, it is a milinfosum dated 41, so it's a slightly later one, on the 9th of May, 1993, and it summarises recent events in the Travnik and western Lasva Valley area, which at this stage was really where most of the activity between HV and ABiH forces was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you look, sir, at the note on this document, that is, the first sentence under the summary?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And there's a reference to a date?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It says you should read this milinfosum in conjunction with the milinfosums from the 1st of June onwards, which contain the detail of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you now, General Duncan, if you can comment on the fact that this document appears to be dated 9 May 1993, it's an Annex to milinfosum number 41 dated 9 May 1993. Can you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It must be wrongly labelled. It can't be May. I think it's June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, what would be the purpose of an Annex such as this one to a milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The purpose of this Annex would enable those people who read it to get a much better idea of what's going on, rather than just taking the snapshots they get every evening from the milinfosum. So what my intelligence officer has put together is a summary of all those recent events so that people who are not aware of what's going on or need to get up to date can read this, and they can then understand what is happening over the period. It gives an idea of what has happened in the past, and a possibility of what might happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was that done on a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was done as required. There was no particular trigger by weeks. It was merely done when we felt there was a need to make sure people knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Mr. Mundis, did the previous document, Exhibit 285, PT01189, referred to an Annex A to it, and I'm particularly interested to see that Annex A to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me make some inquiries about that, Your Honour. I had noticed that yesterday and made some preliminary inquiries. I'm not sure if that document is in the OTP's possession, and I don't believe that it's on the exhibit list, but I will certainly make some inquiries and will provide that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it have to stand alone in the exhibit list as an item or is it part of Annex -- is it part of PT01189?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, it could very well be a part, obviously, since it's referred to, but it did not come up in our system as being attached to this. It might have a sequential ERN number, but we'll make some inquiries on that at the next break and see if we can inform the Trial Chamber at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, at which point, sir, I might as well remind you that you're left with three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now ask the witness, sir, if you've ever heard of a place called Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: In Guca Gora had a large church, and in that church were sheltering a number of Croats who had been surrounded by BiH, and my call signs, which were out on the ground, detected that there was going to be a problem here because these people could well be massacred, as a result of which I deployed a very large force to Guca Gora, to the church, and we managed to eventually, over two days, rescue 187 people who were stuck there, who were put in the back of my armoured vehicles and brought back into the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember on what date this was when they were in this church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I haven't got the date. I can -- the number -- the number "187" is printed on me, but not the date, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Duncan, what steps, if any, were taken with respect to these 187 people who were in that church?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: They were conveyed in the back of my armoured vehicles to the refugee centre in the Lasva Valley, where they were able to meet up with their friends and relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown PT01240. PT01240.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, I would like you to focus your attention on paragraph B of this document, and please tell the Trial Chamber if you know anything about what's described in paragraph B.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Paragraph B describes the situation prior to the evacuation, where we had surrounded -- or were surrounded by Mujahedin elements in some strengths, the group containing Arabic speakers, and were quite hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, what, sir, if anything, can you tell us about these Mujahedin elements?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The Mujahedin elements in Central Bosnia consisted of a number of what I call local Mujahid who were part of the BiH, who had decided to put on clothing and equipment more aligned with Mujahed type people rather than normal soldiers, and that was one element. It was what I call "the locals." There were also a number of elements who came from outside, and I say they came from outside -- they came from outside of the country and into the country and joined almost as mercenaries, and joined up with the ABiH. It is my belief that the reason they did that is because at this stage and later on an awful lot of money was being put into the BiH from outside resources, and the bill for that, I believe, was a requirement to take in to the BiH a number of Mujahedins, both local and imported. They were very hostile at most of times. They formed later on into formed units, and they were used with great effect by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 287.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am cognizant of the time, as well as our Rule 65 ter estimate on this witness. I would ask the Trial Chamber's leave for a little bit more time. I have four more documents, all of which relate to the subject of the Mujahedin, that I would like to cover with this witness, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll deal with one document now, sir, and move on to the remaining three after the recess -- or after the break. I do thank the Trial Chamber. Could we please now see the document PT01116, PT01116.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, General Duncan, can you tell us what you mean when you say, referring to the Mujahedin, "They formed later into formed units and they were used to great effect by the ABiH"? Can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. The Mujahedin became the basis of 7 Muslim Brigade, which was a manoeuvre unit, and because of its -- its makeup, they were very efficient and good soldiers. I say "good" in the effective term. They were very effective soldiers. I wouldn't ever actually put the tag of "good" along side them. However, they were often used, and as part of a plan, if you wished to move forward, and I've stated before or tried to state before, that the ABiH have lots of soldiers but little equipment, and therefore having a unit which has quite good equipment and pretty nasty people, in terms of being able to fight extremely well, would often be used and advertised before an assault went on. So they would say, "7 Muslims" or "The Mujahedin are coming," and people would be very, very frightened, and therefore in terms of shock tactics, they were a very special unit, able to put people's minds at worry about what was going to happen, and then they would follow on with an attack, perhaps, and go through. That enabled a very quick and clean and well-organised force to move the ABiH's forces front line forward and win some more ground, which they did very successfully using these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, if you could now look at the document on the screen in front of you and tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Once again, it is a milinfosum from my battle group, dated the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's then turn, please, to page 3 in English and page 4 in the Bosnian language. And I would ask, General Duncan, if you could please look, when this page comes up, if you could please look at paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. This refers directly to a visit to Zenica by one of my liaison officers, who was able to visit and see the Mujahedin manoeuvre unit in a street there, the commander of which was absent, but the unit spokesman, who comes from Istanbul and therefore was somebody from outside the country who had been brought in, stated those five points there. He stated the strength of his unit, the fact that it is directly subordinate to 3 BiH, but currently there are only 15 soldiers there, that they train themselves, that they are members of -- they are Bosnian Muslims who are members of the unit to encourage to grow beards; and therefore, become more Mujahedin-like than they would normally. They don't believe any intervention by the Western powers will assist them in their plight, the Bosnian plight. And there are a number of nationalities fighting with the Mujahedin, including Australians, Canadians, French, and British.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And General Duncan, my last question before we take a short recess. In paragraph 10(a)(1), where it says: "... directly subordinate to HQ 3 BiH Corps," do you have a comment or can you comment upon that part of this report?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: My comment would be is when you have a specialised unit, such as that organisation of Mujahedins, they have to be used with skill and very carefully; and therefore, they must be controlled at the highest level. In a similar way, whether you have special forces in other armies, those special forces come under high command. It would be very unusual for any force like this of Mujahedins or, if you like, shock troops, to be given just anywhere and which array. You would want to keep them especially for operations where you can get the maximum effort out of them, and that's very important. And because they can do so much so quickly, you would keep them under the very highest command, and I can understand here they would certainly be under command of the 3rd Corps in Zenica and, I would think, even higher command, because you can't afford to waste that product. It's very important. They are shock troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Duncan. We would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, do I understand you to say that they would not be under the control of lesser officials in the ranks of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, you are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that be a convenient time, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It would indeed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness now be shown PT01312, PT01312.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, can you identify the document that's currently on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. It's a milinfosum 55 dated the 23rd of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go, in this document, to page 3 in both the English and B/C/S versions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I would draw your attention, sir, to paragraph 8 in the English version of this document, and I would ask you if you could please take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while the witness is doing that, Your Honour, I note for the record that the Bosnian version of this document, the translation has two paragraph 3s, and as a result it's paragraph 7 in the Bosnian version, for the benefit of General Delic and the Defence. The translation is mis-numbered, so we're looking at paragraph 8 in English and paragraph 7 in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, have you had a chance to review paragraph 8 of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you comment upon what's written in paragraph 8 of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very significant document, in that the first part, where it begins with paragraph 8, is a report from the European Community Monitoring Mission where a woman has been attacked by -- wearing inappropriate clothes, and that's obviously an incident that's happened, perpetrated, I assume, by somebody in the Mujahedin, but I think more important is the comment which I think was put together very succinctly by my intelligence officer. It is very significant: "Whether they are under the effective control of 3 Corps or not has been a topic of some debate. This cell believes they are under effective control. They are invariably found at the point of 3 Corps main effort," which I talked about with main efforts earlier on: "That the Mujahedin are clearly capable of extreme acts as demonstrated by the attacks in Zenica and the Guca Gora desecration of the church," which I didn't mention before, and it says: "The labelling of them as uncontrollable is a convenient means of deflecting criticism ..." And I entirely agree with that comment. I think it's a very significant comment of my intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Duncan, why do you say that? Why do you think that's a significant comment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I say it's a significant comment because Simon would have put all this -- Simon Harrison would have put all this together, and from that he has deduced those comments which he has made, which I think are very good. You know, it is easy to take criticism away from -- you know, it's so easy to push something on the side and put it away, but actually he says there, you know, this is a very cunning way of doing business, very good way of doing -- and classic use of special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask this document be admitted into evidence, but I see there's a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you, Witness, regarding a statement you made before the break, just before we took the break. You stated, and I'm translating from English, you stated: "I understand that they were under the command -- they were placed under the command of the 3rd Corps in Zenica." I would think that they would even be under a higher command." And now you're telling us that your own intelligence officer wrote this comment on the same topic. Therefore, what I would like to know is whether this is an opinion or a fact that are you conveying to us. Is it a fact or an opinion from you and from your intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, it is a -- it is a comment from my intelligence officer, but I think it's a very subtle comment, in that it explains that the labelling of them as being uncontrollable is a very convenient excuse, very convenient excuse. So I agree with his comment. And I really can't add any more to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing. Therefore, you believe, you think, that it is the reality, but that's your opinion; that's what you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I think it's reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be clear, General, an excuse for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's not a -- it's not a clear-cut business, this at all. You can use your special forces in various ways. You can use them as shock troops. You can use them to terrify people. You can use them to just -- to be there in some cases. And I just think that you will use them in the best possible way that you can and hold them at the highest level for things, and that is why this is being done. If it's being put out as propaganda, it's very good propaganda. If it's being put out that it's convenient, it's very -- it's very -- it works a number of ways, and you can -- and you can use those thoughts to change what you want to do with your shock troops. I'm sorry to be unclear. It's not a clear-cut business, this. It's a very subtle business of why are they doing this, why are they putting a display on somewhere. Perhaps that's something else. Do they want us to look at that? It's very, very subtle, a subtle use of shock troops, again, and you keep that at the highest level. They may have fooled us here completely, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, and I agree that things are certainly not clear, at least not at this stage of this trial, but what would be, in your view, the interests that the 3rd Corps might have in denouncing control over the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the 3rd Corps would like to use the Mujahedins as part of their corps business, but I suspect that they're not allowed to because they're kept for other things or -- and that's what I think with 3rd Corps doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Going back to the question raised by Judge Lattanzi, you said that the labelling of them as uncontrollable becomes a convenient means of deflecting criticism away from the 3rd Corps. And then you go on -- your intelligence chap goes on to say, "... While still using their proven tactical worth." As you sit there, and let me, by way of preface, acknowledge that in that comment two incidents are mentioned, the Guca Gora attack and the knifing of women. As you sit there, are you able to remember any other incidents in which they were used, subsequent to this date, used by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they had been used by the 3rd Corps, but certainly I can recall a number of events, of a similar type of event, when Mujahedins have said, "Do not wear those clothes," and, "You mustn't do that," wanting to put down what I call a harder line of Muslim than I believe the ABiH -- I mean, the ABiH as an organisation, and I discussed it with senior commanders, I'm supposed to be a Christian, I go to church, deaths, marriages and various other bits and pieces and that's about it. And I think it's the same with the BiH. They are what I call a much, much softer religion, and -- but the import of these harder people changed the dramatics quite effectively, and they hadn't -- before that, you wouldn't get incidents like this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying you're not sure if they had been used by the 3rd Corps. The reason I asked about their use by the 3rd Corps is because this comment leaves the impression with the reader that, in fact, it is the 3rd Corps that is using them, but the 3rd Corps deflects attention from itself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- by describing them as uncontrollable, while still using them. So I'm rather intrigued by your retraction, that you are not saying necessarily they are used by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, they may have been used for a specific purpose by the 3rd Corps and then drawn away again. That would be quite normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A small amount of time, high risk, high impact, and then taken away again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Hence my question: Can you remember an incident, subsequent to this, where they were used in a similar fashion by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't at the moment, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember any other incident, apart from those that have been mentioned so far, whether it's subsequent or previous to this one.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: To be honest, sir, I can't. It's --
