utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel -- I can only apologise. I just cannot -- I just can't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't need to. These computers do go down at times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, General. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would ask that PT01312 be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. PT01312 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask the witness be shown PT01351. That's PT01351.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, do you recognise the document that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. Again it is a milinfosum. This case dated -- 59, 27th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go to the second page in both the English and Bosnian languages, please, and focusing on the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see paragraph 10 that begins: "ORBATS"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us what "ORBATS" refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: "ORBATS" is a shortening form of "Order of Battle," and therefore if you're laying out the enemy that you think you've got, you find out their order of battle, and "ORBAT" merely is a shortening of that, so it describes what's going on in terms of various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you then look, sir, at paragraph 10, where there's a reference to Franjo Nakic, deputy commander, OZ Central Bosnia? Do you know who Mr. Nakic was, and can you tell us what position he held?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of Central Bosnia, and I had a number of conversations with Nakic during -- during my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: What does "OZ" refer to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: "Op. Zone."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "Op. Zone Central Bosnia," what military force are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We're talking about the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which of the parties to the conflict in the Lasva Valley, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The ops. -- well, the ops. zones were ABiH units, as far as I'm aware, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, if you remember: Was Mr. Nakic with the ABiH or with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: He was with the HVO. I'm sorry, I didn't get -- he was with the HVO, very firmly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please take a look at paragraph 10, and I unfortunately, it carries over onto the next page, so we'll have to switch the page, and I'd ask you to look at that, and we'll ask you to comment upon what's contained in paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, have you had an opportunity to read this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on what's contained in this paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The first part, the comment from Nakic describes that he believes there were three subordinate battalions under the brigade headquarters and that they had been infiltrated by a number of, what I call externals, who had come in and joined the 7 Muslim Brigade, and that stands as his own -- as his comment as an HVO officer. For the second part, is initially somewhat confusing for everybody here, I suspect. It is the ORBAT -- the Order of Battle of 7 Muslim Brigade as described down there, and that is an assessment of the cell. It is not fact, it's an assessment of the cell. And what they're saying is below the paragraph where it starts "7," and this is a Muslim headquarters based in Zenica with a commander, a deputy, and a security man, and I assume the deputy is not filled at the moment. That's the second one down. They then have 1st Battalion 7th, which is in Travnik, with a Commander of Asim Korcic. And then "UI" is "Unidentified," so it's an unidentified company in Travnik, an unidentified company in Mehurici, an unidentified company in Ravno Rostovo, and that completes the 1st Battalion. And then the 2nd Battalion has a commander and only one unidentified element which is down there in cell Sedzeno Polici [phoen]; and then the Battalion similarly with just a commander. So that is given the order of battle, as it were, that's laid out, and this is a comment assessing that the Mujahedin are subsumed within 7MMB, and the remark about Nakic seems to confirm this. But, again, I remember this is a comment from my intelligence officer, but I think that's a pretty straightforward comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Duncan. We'd ask, Your Honours, that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit number 290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I would now ask that the witness be shown P01451, P01451, page 1 of both the English and Bosnian versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, can you recognise the document that's visible on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, it is a PWO milinfosum number 100, dated the 7th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I would ask you, sir, to focus your attention on paragraph 3 of this document. And if you could please take a look at that, and then I will ask you to comment upon that paragraph. Sir, have you had an opportunity to read this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any comment upon what's contained in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm not sure entirely, but I think Sipic is a part of the 3rd Corps. I think he was a deputy commander. He may not have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if you were to look at the first sentence of paragraph 2, that might refresh your recollection as to Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I am right on that, then. He's 306 Brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And with respect to paragraph 3, sir, do you have any comment to add about what's contained in this milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It is interesting, because clearly Sipic is concerned that there would be a problem if members of my unit went to visit without an escort, because they would be guaranteed a hostile response, which is not a terribly good thing to do. And, secondly, the comment there is that -- that the group is clearly hostile and that they are very much under command. They're a part of the ORBAT that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Duncan. I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit number 291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we, during the course of the last break, were able to identify and locate Annex A to milinfosum number 40 of 8 June 1993. I provided a copy to the Defence at the break and discussed this with Mr. Robson. He would have no objection to that document going in with a caveat, with the caveat, that you will recall Exhibit 286, which was Annex B to milinfosum number 41. Mr. Robson indicated that if we were to also bring in Annex A to milinfosum number 41, and I again was able to, with the assistance of Mr. Neuner, obtain copies of that Annex, which I -- I've got both of those here in the courtroom. And Mr. Robson will correct me if what I've just said is wrong, but my understanding was as long as both of those annexes were presented to the witness, the Defence would not object to those documents coming in, although they weren't technically on the Prosecution's exhibit list, although as Your Honour, the Presiding Judge indicated, obviously Annex A to the exhibit might very well be considered part of that exhibit, in any case. But with that lengthy explanation, perhaps if these remaining two documents could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, do you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I concur with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They may be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What we have, unfortunately, only is hard copies of these documents. I do have multiple copies of them, and if the usher could assist in distributing these. Perhaps -- I don't have many questions, but I do note, at least, Annex A has, again, a number of military acronyms, and it might be helpful simply to have the witness tell us what those are for the benefit of everyone so that we all can understand what's contained in Annex A to milinfosum number 41 of 9 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, I misspoke, Annex A to milinfosum number 40 dated 8 June 1993. And perhaps if the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, I'm going to ask you to put the document Annex A to milinfosum number 40, dated 8 June 1993 on the machine, the ELMO machine to your right, so that we all can ensure that we're looking at the same document. Now, sir, I apologise for not having shown you this document earlier, and if there's any information I'm asking you about that you don't remember or don't recall, just simply indicate that. But let's start, sir, with whether or not you recognise this document that's been placed in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I certainly recognise it as a milinfosum from my unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, under the heading "Time," there -- under each of the entries are six-digit numbers. Do you know, sir, what those six-digit numbers refer to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: They normally refer to a date/time group, but I'm not sure which date/time group we're on at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if it would assist you, again we're looking at a document dated 8 June 1993. I don't know if that assists you in any way.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It doesn't, I'm afraid. And that's -- ah, I'm with you now. I think -- I think it is obviously a timeline down the right-hand side, and therefore the detail is of an engagement going on, and somebody has recorded the dates all the way down, which is pretty straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And so the "08" would refer to what?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Well, "0803" I think refers to the time of the event happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then the last two digits?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The last two digits are -- I'm not sure what they would be. It may be shorthand for some other stuff, but I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could perhaps lead the witness. I believe we could clarify this matter. Again, in light of the fact that he hasn't seen this document recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, I would suggest to you, and if I'm completely out of line, sir, simply tell me, I would suggest that the "08" refers to "8 June" and the four digits afterwards would refer to the time.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd probably concur with that. In fact, I would concur with that, so it's back to front. Yeah, so the "08" running all the way down is the 8th of June, and the four next digits are the timelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, again, I'm only going to be asking you about some of the abbreviations on the document so that it's of assistance to the Trial Chamber. The first line under "080350", can you tell us what "ARTY" refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It refers to "Artillery."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the abbreviation "SAF"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Is "Small Arms Fire," so that would be rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the next line, "080540" we again see "C/S"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That would be a call sign. So a call sign which is deployed out of camp is reporting in that there's fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The entry "080630," at the end of that line, again we see again "ARTY/MBRL." Can you tell us what that would refer to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which line again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "080630. The guard reports ..." At the end of that line.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Artillery and multi-barrel rocket-launcher rounds. Artillery and multi-barrel rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Then if we could go down to the entry "080810: "Outgoing rounds reported ...," the second line of that entry: "Approximately 1 times RD every minute."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It's one round, it's a shell every minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the entry "080830," we see a reference to you reporting something.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it says: "200 times CAS."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's "Casualties."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then go -- if we could have the document moved down so that we can see the bottom half of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at the entry "081115: Approximately 50 - 60SA rounds." What would that "SA" refer to.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Again, that's "Small Arm," "Small Arms."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The entry "081215." It says: "1ZU-23-2AAMG." Can you tell us, if you know, sir, what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It is a designation used for an anti-aircraft machine-gun but used in a ground role. So what you're doing is using a cannon, an anti-aircraft cannon, to use on a ground role as opposed to its normal role, which would be to shoot down aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, what the "ZU-23-two" refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It's a former Soviet weapons system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then go, sir, to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The entry under "081815" towards the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if we could have the bottom half of the document, please, 081815.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It says: "A call sign reports that the Dolac CP ..." Can you tell us what "CP" refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It refers to check-point. Dolac was a check-point, and the armed mine, yes, was discarded or disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the entry, sir, under "082145," the second line: "30 times 7.62-mm Coax ...," can you tell us what that refers to, please?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That would refer to a firing of one of my units from the chain gun which is fitted to the Warrior armoured vehicle, and it would be 30 rounds of 7.65-millimetre, coax returned. The machine-gun is aligned on the same line as the main element, so it will hit the same target. But that's fired 30 rounds from its cannisters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I beg your pardon. What do you say "Coax" stands for? After "7.62-millimetre"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, "coaxial." I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Coaxial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe that's all the abbreviations on the document. We would ask, Your Honours, that this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And perhaps if the final document, which is marked or labelled "Annex A to 1 PWO milinfosum number 41" dated the 9th of June could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Duncan, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, that's again a milinfosum, in this case 41, dated the 9th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, I note just a few abbreviations in this document. We'll try to explain those, if that's possible. Could you please look at the entry 9 June at 0725 hours. That would be "090725." Can you look at the very last line, where it says: "The Dutch TPT BN," and tell us what, if you know, that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It refers to the Dutch Transport Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then, sir, in the next line, "090742," at the end of the first line, "FP." Do you know, sir, what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It stands for "Firing Point."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the next line: "090805, Sporadic SA/HMG ..."?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That is: "Sporadic small arms and heavy machine-gun ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The entry under "090930", in the fourth line, we see: "Approximately 12 times TPS equipped with RPG-7." Do you know, General Duncan, what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: "TPS" is referring to the number of troops, so there were 12 soldiers, and "RPG-7" is a shoulder-launched anti-armour weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what does "RPG" stand for?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: "Rocket-Propelled Grenade-7," which is numenclature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that covers all of the abbreviations in this document. We would ask that this be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, sir. Thank you very much, and thank you to the Trial Chamber for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Yes, Mr. Robson. I see you standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm just waiting for my lectern. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Duncan. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be questioning you on behalf of General Rasim Delic this afternoon. If I could begin with some preliminary questions. Could you just confirm for the Trial Chamber that you have testified before this Tribunal on three prior occasions, in the Blaskic case in 1998, in the Kordic case in 1999, and the Hadzihasanovic case in 2004?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of your evidence, you made a reference to the BiH forces, meaning Muslim forces. Mr. Duncan, were you aware that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that they're a multi-ethnic army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you knew that its ranks were comprised of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, but I would add the derider that the majority of them are, to my knowledge, are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, it's right that when you left Bosnia in 1994, you wrote an article called "Operating in Bosnia"; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember it, though, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in that article, it's right to say that you defined the mission for your battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own as: "To create conditions whereby aid could be delivered into and through our area of responsibility." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as part of that mission statement, you considered that it was important for the regiment to gather information so that Brit-Bat could create those conditions for aid to be delivered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. That was essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if you're not able to help us with this, please say so, but when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April of 1994, it's right that the blockade of the Travnik region by the HVO had been in place for a considerable period of time? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Before I arrived, there was no blockade, as I was aware of it, and it was a much more benign environment, and there didn't seem to be any animosity between the two armed forces at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, again, if you can't help us, please say so, but isn't it the case that there had been a number -- there had been conflict between the HVO and the BiH prior to your arrival in Bosnia in April 1993, and consequently this has had the effect of restricting the movement of the Bosnian Army and depriving Bosnian Muslims in certain places of food?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I mean, the only conflict I knew that had gone on was that -- was Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but before it disappears, I believe on line 5 of page 60, that should be April of 1993, not April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 5 of page 60. Sorry, can you say that line again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Line 5 of page 60, there's a reference to the General's arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April of 1994, and I believe that should be 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can quickly clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You arrived in April 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes, on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could -- if the witness could please be shown Exhibit 283. There's no Bosnian translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, we can see here a milinfosum dated the 5th of June, 1993. I would just like to refer your attention down to point 3. Obviously, this is in the section headed "Travnik." And if I can just read out the beginning of this paragraph, it says: "At 051000, the Travnik LO attended a meeting in the Travnik PT building, the location of the joint HQ ..." And then later, if we move down about halfway down this paragraph, it then goes on to say: "Merdan claimed that 18 Muslims had been massacred in the village of Bukovica, GR 1402, and that something similar had occurred in Radojcici, GR 1801." First of all, do you recall this report, about the HVO -- it mentions the HVO attack on Bukovica?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I don't recall it, no. I don't believe I was -- I was not at that meeting, and I don't recall that particular comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And again if you can't recall, please say so, but do you remember did Brit-Bat react at all, when that information was passed, that Muslims had been massacred in Bukovica village?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: In terms of taking that report back to my headquarters, which is what would have been done because it's now appeared on this form, and there is a comment after it which says there's no collateral for it, as a comment, not a fact, so we registered that something had been reported but there didn't appear to be any collateral for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And by "collateral," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: More confirmation of what had happened rather than just a bold statement which Merdan had claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Duncan, and if you can't say, obviously please tell us that, that it was this HVO attack on Bukovica on the 5th of June, resulting in the death of those Muslims and the capture of the village's inhabitants, that was the trigger for the ABiH's counter-attack along the Bila Valley on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I can't physically confirm the dates, but, you know, there are -- what actually sparked it off, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. Certainly, it's right, isn't it, that the attack on the 8th of June was limited to the Bila Valley and not the Lasva Valley, as you mentioned in your examination-in-chief? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would agree that the -- that the conflict started at the western end of the Lasva Valley. I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that that is the Bila Valley region?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, it's simply wrong to say, as you suggested in your examination-in-chief, that both sides were involved in ethnic cleansing, running people out of their homes and killing them, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I -- I saw ethnic cleansing on both sides during my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is very difficult to establish sometimes who's done what and where, but it was a -- a prevalent activity, and it was done occasionally --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: -- to next door neighbours, strangely enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking what you tell us, but we are talking about the 8th of June, the events at that time, at this stage. Now, I'd like to turn to a different topic, and that is cooperation between Croat and Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown document D220. I beg your pardon, it's D260. Perhaps just to explain the document whilst it's way -- whilst we're waiting for it, it's a milinfosum, number 39, dated the 7th of June, 1993. We can see halfway down of page 1, it comments upon events in Travnik. Now, what I'm interested in is over at page 2 at point number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'll just read out some extracts from this paragraph. It starts off saying: "A normally reliable BiH source offered the following explanation of certain events in Travnik. He claimed that an order was issued by the Travnik HVO at 061900 ordering the evacuation of Croats to Ovcarevo from surrounding villages." Moving down a little, it then goes on to say: "At 070130 the people, including HVO soldiers who had discarded their uniforms, moved out of Ovcarevo and reputedly crossed the Serb lines to Babanovac. The source claims that this was part of a well-organised agreement by which the HVO would surrender their positions in the defence of Travnik and Turbe to the BSA." Now, just to again clarify, Mr. Duncan, the BSA is the Bosnian Serb Army, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, yes it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that the explanation from that BH source was indeed correct and in fact cooperation had taken place between the HVO and BiH Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: There were two results about people moving out. One was that people would have gone across to the BSA, and the other that people were hiding in the woods and hadn't actually disappeared at all, and had just been forced out of their houses. Those are the only two points I know from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It actually refers to that later on down in the document. People weren't moving out of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you. I just want to find out. You're talking of, Mr. Robson, of the HVO cooperating with the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document talks of surrender. Are those two words used synonymously?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer that, but perhaps if I could put the question to the witness and explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: First of all, if I can begin -- go back a little, have you seen this document before, this milinfosum dated the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I have seen this document before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what I've asked you is: Were you aware that cooperation was taking place between the HVO and Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I was only aware that if there was going to be a movement of people out, they would either go out across the Bosnian Serb Army lines or into the woods. That's all I knew. But it would be logical to assume that there was some sort of liaison between the Bosnian Serb Army to let people across their front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Duncan, that around that time large numbers of Bosnian Croat civilians crossed Serb lines in the Croat region; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would -- I would not be able to put a finger on the -- on the numbers, and although the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: -- the milinfosum puts it here as about 3.000. That's quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you wouldn't be able to put your finger on the figures, but you are aware that an officer of your regiment has reported that 3.000 Croats have crossed Serb borders. Could that sort of movement take place without cooperation between the HVO and the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I think it's quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that around this time when this cooperation took place, the HVO simply deserted large sections of the front line that they'd been holding against the Bosnian-Serb forces? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when the HVO deserted those front line sections, it's correct, isn't it, that a vacuum was created which the Bosnian Army suddenly had to fill to prevent the Bosnian-Serb forces moving in and claiming that territory; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: My colleagues are telling me to slow down, so I'm going to heed their advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can see he'd been trying to do that for a long time, and I'm pleased he's finally getting through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the topic of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Duncan, that it was the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian Army and its subordinate units that Brit-Bat mostly dealt with?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I tried to be -- keep it in balance between dealing with HVO and 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps that was me being unclear, but what I was trying to get at was this: Within the Bosnian Army, it was almost exclusively the 3rd Corps that you had your dealings with?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And no other?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, because you will recall in my previous statement I had a plan for gathering information, which meant that I personally would be dealing with the corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether there's communication between the two, but I suppose what Mr. Robson is trying to suggest is that you didn't, for instance, deal with the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian Army, and you didn't deal with the 1st Corps; you were mainly dealing with the 3rd Corps within the larger Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you're trying to say, Mr. Robson, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that Brit-Bat's area of operations broadly corresponded to the 3rd Corps' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Technically, my area of responsibility went from Romboci to Tuzla, and the aid group through there, and we were therefore very focused on the aid route. And if I could remind you, the aid route went from Novi Bila -- sorry, Guca Gora and then got to Novi Travnik, and then went through the Lasva Valley up to Zenica. So that part of activity that was going on in Travnik was not threatening the aid route, which was our primary aim and task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, so parts of your area of operations were outside of the 3rd Corps. You told us that you met with Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. Were you aware that it was only in November of 1992 that he was appointed as the commander of the 3rd Corps and, in fact, the 3rd Corps only began functioning sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that because it was before my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at the time that the 3rd Corps was formed, there were extremely difficult conditions in place with the Bosnian Army defending itself from Serb and, indeed, HVO aggression?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. They were in -- it was a difficult -- very difficult time for them, yes, and it's something I discussed with Enver.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from what you saw, the soldiers of the Bosnian Army were very poorly equipped, weren't they, and lacked decent weapons and uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: A little earlier during examination-in-chief, we referred to a milinfosum dated the 6th of June, 1993, and we looked at how the Bosnian-Serb Army was equipped with Howitzers, 50 tanks, and so on. It's right, isn't it, that the Army of both Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't have any sort of equipment like that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that the 3rd Corps had to defend a front line against the Serbs extending to around 300 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. I would assume that you're talking about the western front line on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you accept that that is, in reality, a huge front line to defend?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, it is a huge front line to defend, in a similar manner that my battalion was asked to do 180 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. And it's right, isn't it, that the ARBiH's task was to become significantly harder when the HVO commenced its cooperation with the Serb forces and abandoned its sections of the front line?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I would agree with that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's also right to say, isn't it, that at the time that the Bosnian Army was trying to establish itself, there was a UN arms embargo in place which severely constrained the possibility of the Bosnian Army obtaining weapons from outside?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, and I discussed that with Enver at detail, and I seem to remember at some stage during that detail I promised to give him some books and pamphlets on how to organise an army, which he found quite useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me when I say that the task to form the 3rd Corps, comprising around 30.000 men, must have been a virtually impossible assignment for Commander Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It would be a significant challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, despite all of those difficulties, it's right to say that the 3rd Corps did take some steps to ensure that international humanitarian law was respected within the corps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and indeed one of the pamphlets we gave them discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you two documents that touch upon this issue. The first is Defence document D280. And while we're waiting for this to come on screen, perhaps I can just explain that this is an order from Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic, dated 3rd of February, 1993, and it's to all brigade groups and municipal defence staffs. It's a long document so I'm not going to read all of it, but perhaps if I could just read a couple of extracts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What this document from February states is: "There have been occurrences of looting and burning of objects, as well as imprisonment of civilians in the course of combat activities so far. These actions were perpetrated by individuals who do not respect orders and instructions issued by their superiors. We do not want to build an army using the same methods and ways as the aggressor. We want to build an army with a humane conception of warfare that will respect and adhere to all the Geneva Conventions and the UN Charter." And perhaps if I can just read briefly from point number 1 by way of example. We can see that Commander Hadzihasanovic says: "Strictly prohibit all units of RBH Army in the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility from imprisoning unarmed civilians, looting property, and burning down infrastructural facilities." My question to you, Mr. Duncan, is: Is this the sort of instructions that you would expect a responsible commander to issue to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Entirely. I would expect nothing else, if you wish to give me an army that's going to be effective. Sadly, I don't think that both HVO and ARBiH held to those tenets throughout this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Duncan, that wasn't my question. I'd be very grateful if you could please restrict your answer to the question I'm putting to you, and perhaps restrain from putting your comments to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: In that case, yes, it would be a good thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, could I tender this document for admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Next, please, could we refer to document D264. D264. Whilst we're waiting for it appear on the screen, I can perhaps just explain. It's a milinfosum number 127, dated the 6th of March, 1993, and it's the top part of this document I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we look at this document, Mr. Duncan, can you just confirm that this document was produced by the Cheshire Regiment, the battalion that preceded yours?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes, because it's got its flick on as being a Cheshire milinfosum, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Robson, don't we have a B/C/S copy? I think Mr. Delic would like to see what's being talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid that we don't have a B/C/S version here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't. Okay. If we don't, we don't. Is it possible to generate one at some stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, it may be. What you'll notice from this document is that the majority of it is in B/C/S. It's just the introductory part that I'm interested in, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Delic doesn't feel disadvantaged, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps just before I move to the document, Mrs. Vidovic, by way of explanation, tells me that we did request this, but we've been unable to obtain a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the document, it states "1. Sarajevo": "BiH officers have been issued a small rules for the armed forces handbook, "Pravila Oruzanih Snaga," dated 01 August 1992 and approved by President Alija Izetbegovic. The book covers many aspects of BiH procedures; e.g., general discipline, uniform, insignia, ranks, weapon handling," et cetera, and then perhaps if I just move to the bottom of this paragraph within the comment section it states: "It is reportedly on issue to all BDE and BN commanders." By "BDE" and "BN," does that mean brigade and battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, were you aware that the Bosnian army had distributed such a handbook to the commanders of different units?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, because at that stage I wasn't in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it's not something that you found out about later, once you actually arrived in the country?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I saw it, yes, later on, but at this stage I didn't yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, despite all the difficulties faced by the Bosnian Army, does this demonstrate to you that the Bosnian Army Command was taking serious steps to professionalise its army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this document could please be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, during your testimony, you commented upon communications, and I'd just like to explore the basis for what you told the Tribunal, if I may. First of all, it's correct, isn't it, that during the time that you were deployed to Bosnia, land line telephones weren't functioning in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: They -- that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as to radio communication, it's right, isn't it, that was also pretty dreadful; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would agree that it was difficult, but there is a difference between -- technical difference between VHF and UHF and other forms. Some of it is easy, the HF and VHF, but some of it isn't, and it requires the skills and training of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that when the JNA retreated from Bosnia and Herzegovina in May of 1992, they destroyed all of the radio relay stations throughout Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, the radio relay stations in the Lasva Valley area, and I call that area, were still functioning and functioned throughout most of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right to say, isn't it, that the HVO had equipment which could block radio transmissions by the Bosnian Army, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It probably had, yes. On the balance of probability, I would say it probably had, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown a document. It's Exhibit 86. This is a daily operations report dated the 11th of April, 1993, from the commander of the 306 Brigade, Esad Sipic, to the 3rd Corps Operations Centre and OG West Command. Now, it's the third paragraph under point 2 that I'm interested in. Perhaps before we read this, perhaps briefly if we could just -- we see on the B/C/S version on the bottom through "Komandant, Esad Sipic." If we can move down, please, a little in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What it states is: "Communication with OG West Command has been practically nonexistent in the past 10 days. This should be resolved immediately. The lines with OG West Command are down or occasionally very bad so that it is not possible to check, let alone work. Therefore, we are not able to carry out your order number 017493 of 9 April 1993. The reason is that we are 18 kilometres away from the Travnik communications centre, and we have no means for sending a message three times a day." So first of all, Mr. Duncan, were you aware that the 306 Mountain Brigade operated in the OG West's area of responsibility at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you accept that this report from the commander to its superior command clearly demonstrates that communication from the field was not effective and, indeed, it hadn't been so for some time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm surprised about this report, because as I mentioned before, I was aware that the relays were all working and worked during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could ask, if you had this sort of information, if it had been presented to you, perhaps your assessment of the ability to communicate by radio in that region would have been somewhat different?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It is difficult to communicate in that region, yes, and those same problems of communication occurred with ourselves, given that we had more sophisticated radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we put this document away, perhaps if we could just refer to the paragraph above this. It's not to do with communications, but what it states is: "Logistics support of the unit is bad, which made it practically impossible for us to carry out regular jobs. The cause is a lack of," something illegible, "fuel, lubricants, and spare parts for the vehicles. A constant problem has also been the lack of weapons, ammunition, and clothing, which we have already warned about earlier."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Duncan, that that paragraph accurately reflects the poor conditions that you witnessed, whilst you were in Central Bosnia, for the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's quarter past. Perhaps this might be a good opportunity to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you still have more questions about this document or do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I've finished with this document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall we admit it before we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's already been admitted. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's an exhibit, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's an exhibit we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, we were talking about communications, and during your examination-in-chief you mentioned that one of the reasons that you concluded that there were good communications in Bosnia was something that you saw when you had lunch with the corps commander. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you said you had lunch with the corps commander, was that Commander Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, it -- yes, Enver Hadzihasanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what you had to say was: "We had a lunch in a hotel. The next door was quite clearly a communication system back to wherever you want to be." And that was at page 21, line 16. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on the 8th and 9th of May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall making or giving a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecution on the 8th or 9th of May of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: If it was one of the -- yes, that I've given before, one of the statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Because if I could perhaps just refresh your memory, at page 8 of that document you discuss the lunch that you had with Commander Hadzihasanovic, and what you said about this lunch was the following: "When I arrived at the restaurant, I observed a portable command truck which was parked close to the restaurant. I observed a series of antennae on the back -- on the truck," sorry,"which again displayed to me that the 3rd Corps did have efficient communications." So perhaps you could first of all clarify, what was this communications system that was next door to the restaurant? Was it a truck or was it a building?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It was a truck equipped with aerials and, in particular, a high-frequency aerial, which means you can transmit over great distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, it's right, isn't it, that this was a very elderly ex-JNA vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, but ex-JNA vehicles are actually extremely robust and strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I'm right to say that you didn't enter that vehicle, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, I didn't enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you didn't assess its capabilities or speak to anyone about it, about its performance, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: At that moment, no. But as I mentioned, it had a high-frequency aerial, which enables you to transmit great distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the information you told us related to what you saw within the 3rd Corps' area of responsibility, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What you saw and what you told us about today related to things that were limited to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At no stage did you ever travel to Sarajevo and visit the Supreme Command headquarters or any of its forward command posts outside the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: A little earlier in your testimony, in relation to communications with Sarajevo, what you told the Court was you felt you could get an answer very quickly. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a feeling is not a solid basis upon which to conclude that there was an efficient communications system in place with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I was in -- I have communications with Sarajevo at the time, and there were officers from BH Command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "I have communications"? Do you mean that you were using your communication?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Not at the time, no, but I had -- I had, in the field, I had communications from where I was most of the time back to Sarajevo, if I wished, using HF.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could just clarify this. Well, perhaps we can look at a document. It's Defence document 267 which deals with this issue. And whilst we're waiting for that document, I can explain that it's a milinfosum dated the 28th of June, 1993. If we go halfway down this page, we can see the heading "Meetings," and what it states here is that: "The fourth meeting of the joint command, born of the 18 June cease-fire agreement, took place in Brit-Bat Main with the following attendance:" And we can see under the heading "BiH," it states "Siber" and "Karic"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Were you familiar with both of those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can we confirm the reference to "Karic" is to Vehbija Karic, who was a member of the Bosnian Army General Staff; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I wasn't -- no, I wasn't aware of that. Not of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can turn over on to page 2, please, it's point 4 that I'm interested in. If I could just read a couple of extracts from this paragraph. It states: "After the above agreements had been made, Karic spoke for the first time at the meeting." If we move down, it goes on to say: "He personally knew many of the HVO delegation from his former service in the JNA, and stated his incredulity that things had changed so much in the last 15 months, that the situation in Bosnia was as it is." And then at the bottom of this paragraph, there is a comment that states: "The impression given by Karic's speech is that his previous understandings of the realities of Central Bosnia was fragile in the extreme. Given that he is in a position to be able to brief the president, this suggests that the passage of information on the area and the understanding of it is not particularly good. Comment ends." Now, Mr. Duncan, would you agree that that comment, made by one of your officers in the regiment, suggests that no matter what the state of communications were like within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, communication from Central Bosnia to the General Staff HQ in Sarajevo was not very good?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it -- that's what the comment says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic, if I may. It's right to say, isn't it, -- sorry, I beg your pardon. Before we go any further, please, could that be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document D267 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get clarification. Sir, to what does this comment relate, talking about his understanding of the realities of Central Bosnia was fragile in the extreme? Does it relate to communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're talking to me? I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume this was saying that the information in the area of understanding was not very good, but that's not just restricted to radio. Often staff officers come from headquarters and discover that they haven't got the truth, and it's only by coming down they can understand what's going on. And in that, in this case, I think the realities of Central Bosnia were suddenly revealed, as it were, and it was -- they are having a very difficult time. I would agree with that. But I think the communication is still there. It's a lack of logistics and a lack of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say it's a lack of logistics and a lack of equipment, are you saying that's what the comment speaks to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It speaks to logistics and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It speaks to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and to communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And communication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Moving to this new topic, Mr. Duncan: It's correct, isn't it, that it was common practice for the HVO in Central Bosnia to make false or exaggerated claims in relation to the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: With respect to what aspects of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what your question is. You're asking to make exaggerated claims. On what, on their performance, on their equipment, on their people, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Rather than answering your question, Mr. Duncan, what I'll do is perhaps show you two documents, and then we can discuss that. The first document -- and, Your Honour, I think at this stage it would be prudent of me to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd ask to see Defence document D269. While we're waiting for this document to appear, perhaps if I could just explain that this is a document to the UN BH Command based at Kiseljak. It's dated the 21st of June, 1993. It's an HQ BH Command daily infosum. Perhaps if we could just scroll down this page a little to just to confirm what I've told the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does it come from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, if we could just go back up. What we can see, in the top two -- top four squares, we can see who it's addressed to. The left-hand square shows us that. And on the right-hand side, that square tells us it's from HQ BH Command-Kiseljak. I'm so sorry, I apologise if I said earlier it was to the Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, have you seen this type of report before?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Have you? Perhaps if you can turn to page 2, please, point 4. It's in the lower half of the page. There we go. We can see at point 4 it states "Brit-Bat Sector," and the second paragraph, in the section (a), deals with Kakanj. And what it states is "Freng-Bat reported that the HVO had told the Croats the Haljinci Valley that 2.000 Mujahedin were heading towards them, so they moved to Vares." First of all, perhaps we can clarify, who and what is"Freng-Bat"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Freng-Bat is the French engineer Battalion based on Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you actually recall this report then?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because it's issued from BH headquarters, so I would have seen it. I was somewhat surprised when I saw it, because it's issued from a very junior officer and -- released by a relatively junior officer, which is quite a surprise with a headquarters of the size of BH Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, that junior officer had obviously received information from the HVO that enabled him to make this entry; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, I suspect that that junior officer had got information from a number of milinfosums across the pitch and has attempted to produce a product.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is speculation, isn't it, Mr. Duncan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Well, I know the officer. It's Chambers, isn't it, Guy Chambers, who's done that, his report, if you go up it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It's relatively junior -- a major, a junior officer in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps so I can understand, Mr. Duncan, because Guy Chambers held the rank of major, this somehow made his reports less reliable so that they should not be trusted; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, not at all. I'm saying that such a report would have been signed off at a high -- should have been signed off at a high level, because somebody higher may have disagreed with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at what this document says about the Mujahedin. As I say, it's the HVO: "Freng-Bat reported the HVO had told the Croats that 2.000 Mujahedin were heading towards them ..." During your time in Central Bosnia, you did see one single foreign Mujahedin fighter, did you, let alone 2000?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Me? I saw-- I've seen certainly seen at least two or three. I'm not saying hundreds, because I don't go out on the ground and deal with these people every day. There are others that would see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. You are saying that you have seen foreign Mujahedin fighters?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I believe them to be foreign Mujahedin fighters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll explore this in a little more detail in a while, but according to what you've told the Tribunal on earlier occasions, you've never seen a foreign Mujahedin during your time in Central Bosnia; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: If I've stated that, it's on the record, then that's what I'll have to stick with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Coming back to this report, the suggestion that there were 2.000 Mujahedin heading towards these Croats, that was obviously a gross exaggeration, wasn't it, made by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I think it's a gross exaggeration made by whoever Guy Chambers is who provided this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I just -- I would go back to my -- Your Honour, if I go back to this business, may I make a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I go back to this business of such statements being made which enable people to make the ground for an attack, and therefore, suggesting that 2.000 Mujahedin are coming down is going to put the wind up an awful lot of people and that could be well part of a plan. I'm just -- I'm quite surprised of that number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if Major Chambers had prepared this report, we shouldn't really accept what's contained in it; is that what you're saying, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would -- I would question the report, and we probably did question the report when it came in and put it on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can we look at page 1 of the report, please. If we can go to the top. And we can see the squares, and on the right-hand side there are a number of columns, and we can see in the fourth box down from the top, on the right-hand side, some information.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what we can see in here, drafter, "G2 milinfo," and there's a signature there. That doesn't look like Major Chambers' signature, does it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, but it's next to a major's title, Major Turle, I think it is there, isn't it? I can't-- I don't who Turle is either, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So -- Major Turle. I'd like to return back to page 2, please, on what we were talking about. So would you agree that the author of this piece of information that appears in an UNPROFOR document believed that the HVO was creating disinformation, and in fact it was the HVO that was frightening the Croat population of the Haljinci Valley into believing that an attack by the Mujahedin was imminent? That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's what he said, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it would appear that the HVO has told the Croat civilians that with the purpose that the Croat civilians would move; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So on the face of this report, and I know that you question it, but on the face of this report, would you agree that the HVO appear to be using the concept of the Mujahedin as a propaganda tool to manipulate their own people?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would -- I would -- sorry. That tool has been used by both ABiH and HVO throughout this business. It is part of propaganda machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You have told us earlier on in your evidence how large numbers of Croats left the Travnik region and crossed through Serb lines. 3.000 was the figure you mentioned. Are you aware -- can you help us, is this type of manipulation of Bosnian Croats by the HVO, telling them something to create fear, something that you'd come across during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I believe, in Bosnia, both ABiH and HVO used propaganda and statements to manipulate people and to pave the ground for further advances or whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, I'd like to turn to the issue of the Mujahedin. And in doing so, I'd like to refer you to your testimony in the Hadzihasanovic case, which you gave on the 13th and 14th of May, 2004. Now, during your examination-in-chief on the 13th of May, at page 7293, the Prosecutor asked you the following question. And I should say, Your Honours, that we do have the copies of the transcript on e-court, should we need to look at those documents. What the Prosecutor asked was: "General, did you ever discuss the issue of the Mujahedin with Hadzihasanovic and/or Merdan?" And what you replied was: "Yes, I did. It came up on a number of occasions because I never really knew whether they existed or not." Now, this point was raised during cross-examination on the following day, and it's page 7424 that deals with this, and this time I would ask for the document to be put on the page [sic] as it's a rather long extract. So it's Defence document D294. Okay. If we can scroll down to the bottom half of the page, please, we can see that the question put to you by Defence counsel was the following: "And, General, you did not know -- you had no information about the Mujahedin in terms of who they were, what the money was, what the resupply was, how many there was, how many units there was, where they were, who were their chief, what their relationship with the region was, you knew nothing about that. "How can you today come in this courtroom and say that General Hadzihasanovic had the power to take on an unknown enemy that you don't even know who this enemy is? Please comment on this question, General."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Could I ask you to scroll down a bit further so that people can see my reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at the reply. What you said was: "I have said on a number of occasions that I'm not sure they existed or were used, but the fact that they were around was a powerful tool to be used." And if we can just look on the second page, we'll just see that.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That is exactly the point about the use of the Mujahedin, that's exactly what -- nobody knows what they're going to do or where they're going to be and how they can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Mr. Duncan, that isn't really what you're saying, is it, because your position is unclear. According to what you've said during the Hadzihasanovic case, you couldn't confirm whether or not the Mujahedin actually existed in Central Bosnia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: But it doesn't -- the point is that whether they exist or not, they have an effect. If people perceive that they're there, you don't have to be -- they're having an effect. I didn't know, personally, whether they were or not, as I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, General Delic here is on trial, charged with responsibility for the acts -- the alleged acts of Mujahedin fighters. Whether they existed or not is extremely, extremely important. And according to what you've said here, and indeed what you've told us today, it seems to me that you didn't even know they existed. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The use of Mujahedin, whether they were there or not, is -- I will come back to in a moment, but what I would point out is that their behaviour, or whatever acts were taken in their name, should never be tolerated by anyone. As it happens, as an aside, in the British Army at the moment we're going through a bit of a problem with that business. But I didn't know they were there because I didn't see them, and I put that on -- you have on record. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can interrupt there --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: -- they're like special forces. They don't have to be there on display all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So now you accept that you didn't see them, and what you told us about 15 minutes ago, when you saw two or three of them, that wasn't correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: How do you tell the difference between somebody dressed up in uniform and somebody who's not, somebody dressed up in Mujahedin outfit or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I don't know. You could meet people at Rowbucks who were dressed up as Mujahedin because it's what the local boys wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could clarify another matter. You've told in your evidence today that, "on the one hand the Mujahedin were a special unit," and then you went on to say that "they may have completely fooled us," and then you went on to said that they weren't -- you not sure that they were used by the 3rd Corps at all. It's a confusing situation.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It is a confusing situation. You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution showed you a series of documents relating to the Mujahedin, many of which were milinfosums prepared by your regiment. You explained earlier that the -- that that information, certainly the bulk of it, came from the various officers that worked throughout Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that typically the way your officers gathered information from the members of the HVO and the Bosnian Army involved a lot of drinking of Sljivovica, drinking coffee, and offering cigarettes in exchange for information?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite normal. That's the way things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
