utterances.text: Your liaison officers, when they went out into the field, were accompanied by local people, weren't they, who acted as translators during these meetings with the Bosnian Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes. There would be the driver, a commander, and probably an interpreter, a team of three in a Land Rover.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, even in the calm surroundings of this courtroom, where we have professional interpreters, we've found that sometimes misunderstandings in translation can arise. Would you agree with me that during a wartime situation, where time is precious and Sljivovica and amateur translators are involved, the scope for translation errors was there, it existed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would agree, but we took great cares to make sure we had the best interpreters we could get at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own edification, what is Sljivovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sljivovica is a very strong brandy, alcohol. It is very strong, and it is frequently used throughout that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sir, from what you've told us, the milinfosum was prepared quickly, wasn't it? Your officers had to get the information back for the 6.00 meeting so that your captain could begin compiling the information so it could be issued the next day; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, and I said if there were anything to be corrected, it would be corrected in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, it's right to say, isn't it, that the officers that provided that information from the field to your military information officer, they didn't have the chance to review the document before it was issued out to the field, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, they didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if the information they had passed on to the military information officer was incorrect or had been wrongly understood, there was no opportunity for them to correct that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The 6.00 meeting is when they would be able to correct it, because they would attend the 6.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the information that your men gathered was, in the main, limited to do what they saw and what they heard, wasn't it? And by that, perhaps I should just explain. They didn't have access to any military communications from the Bosnian Army or the HVO, such as orders, directives, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: They also didn't have access to confidential military information held by those parties, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, shall we redact that part of the transcript, starting from --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Starting from line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Obviously, the Statute of the Tribunal emphasizes that trials should be held in an open forum, and I would just perhaps submit that this might be a matter that counsel should both make submissions on before a final decision is taken, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Let's here what the opposite number has to say. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it's not directly on point, I would submit, in light of the witness's prior answer, that perhaps Rule 70 might be an applicable analogy for what's being requested here. I think that the relatively limited scope of what the witness is asking to be redacted is such that this does not in any way render these proceedings to be -- to have the public's interests detrimentally harmed by a slight redaction such as this. I would also say, while I'm on my feet, that on page 21, lines 17 through 21, from the direct examination, also alludes to this point. So I would object to my learned colleague's statement a few moments ago that this is new information. But to the extent that the witness has now indicated that perhaps that information should not be made public, I draw to the Chamber's attention page 21, lines 17 through 21, where similar information is -- was given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Your learned friend has asked that you be allowed to make submissions later. I don't know, is that the sum total of your submission, or would you like to make further submissions later when he makes his?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of course, the problem with that would be that the -- we have a very limited time in order to make redactions, and thus to make submissions later would render it moot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would defeat the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If it assists, the Defence adopts a neutral position here, and we leave it in the hands of the Tribunal -- I beg your pardon. We leave it in the hands of the Chamber as to how it wishes to deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That being the case, then may we redact page 21, lines 14 to 22, and -- sorry, where was this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 96, from line 14 to 23. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when your men attempted to gather information from one of the parties to the conflict, each side often had its own interests and reasons to either supply information or withhold it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you again, Mr. Robson. I'm just being advised, and I think rightly so, that page 21 is already in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So be it, Your Honours. Of course, there is always the possibility that the transcripts, as they'll be made available to the public, could be redacted, notwithstanding the fact that the broadcast has gone out. But again, as with the position by the Defence, I leave that entirely in the Trial Chamber's hands as to whether the Chamber wishes to order a redaction of the actual transcripts which would be posted on the website and made available to the public once they are corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is possible, may we redact the transcripts that are posted to the public. Thank you very much. I'm sorry, Mr. Robson. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do, if I may, is bring to your attention what your predecessor, Colonel Robert Stewart during the Hadzihasanovic trial which occurred on the 31st of January 2005 at page 15.209, and what he said was the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you ask that question, and I'm very sorry to do this to you: According to my notes, this document 294, which was supposed to be on the screen, are you still referring to it or are we done with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it can be taken from the screen, and I won't admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. That's what I wanted to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Duncan. So what your predecessor at Brit-Bat said was, "One of the things I quickly learned in Bosnia was if we don't actually see it ourselves, don't trust it." Would you agree with his comment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It's his comment, the first thing, and I obviously took over from him, and one of the things I did when I took over was to continue that five-level, if you like, intelligence plan to gather information, because people had to see things with their eyes, and that's what my people out on the ground were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, broadly speaking, you would go along with what he had to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as to the purpose for your men gathering information, you said at the beginning of the cross-examination, that it was to enable Brit-Bat to create the conditions whereby aid could be delivered. It's right, isn't it, that Brit-Bat's intelligence requirements in Bosnia were not the same as if it had been a belligerent party to the conflict or, indeed --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, we would tailor the intelligence requirements to the task, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the information that your men gathered was short-term intelligence to enable you to make decisions on how and whether to act on a day-to-day basis as opposed to long-term intelligence; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I would not be reacting on a day-to-day basis. I would be listening to and getting information in. We wouldn't do any knee-jerk reacting, and I would want confirmation, particularly if something was very suspicious or odd or strange or didn't fit in with our patterns, we would like to verify it and perhaps investigate it a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So re-investigation is something that was important to you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've also mentioned during your evidence that the milinfosum represented a snapshot in time of how the situation on the ground appeared at that particular moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that the opinions contained in those milinfosums or that snapshot in time, if you like, could at a later date be changed if new information came to light that revealed a different situation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Are we talking about the opinion or the information that comes before the opinion, because that's quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: There's a difference between what we believe to be fact and a difference between the opinion that came out, and we didn't use the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, and I suppose what I should have asked you is that it's correct to say that at a later stage, both the factual information and the comment that had been expressed in an earlier infosum could both be changed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It would be -- we would change the fact. We probably wouldn't change the comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier on in your evidence, you mentioned the 306th Brigade. I'd like to show you Exhibit 90, if I may. And if I can just explain, this is an official note dated the 28th of May, 1993, from Asim Delalic, the assistant commander of security of the 306th Mountain Brigade, and concerns the death of Sakib Brkic. Perhaps if we can just go to the bottom of the English document just to confirm who it came from. Now, I'd like to read out paragraph 3, and what it says is: "On 25th of May, 1993, a group of Mujahedin who are not under the control of our brigade and are billeted in Mehuric, in the area of responsibility of the 306th Brigade, reconnoitered the Probijeno Brdo sector without having asked for permission and without having informed anyone." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right that this document was prepared not long after the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment arrived in Bosnia; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We arrived on the 5th and I took over on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you accept that this document indicates that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Sorry, run that through again, please. I'm not -- sorry, just the question. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you accept that this document indicates that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document can be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You also mentioned the 7th Muslim Brigade during your testimony, and in respect to this particular brigade I'd like to refer you to the testimony that you gave in the Kordic case, and that was on the 25th of November, 1999, and it was at page number 10.528. Again, we do have -- perhaps the document could be put on the screen. It's D293. Now, while we're waiting for that to come up: You were asked, Mr. Duncan, by Defence counsel during cross-examination whether you knew anything about the relationship between imams and commanders of units. If we can scroll down to the bottom half of this page, please. Again, you can see it's a lengthy question, but in respect of that question, your response was: "I can't remember ever meeting an imam on any of my visits to any ABiH unit. I think, sir, you will be aware of an organisation called the 7th Muslim Brigade. Whether this is fact or fiction, I don't know. These were hard-line or purported to be hard-line religious zealots with the Mujahedin who had apparently had come from outside, but I cannot -- I never saw 7th Muslim Brigade or saw anyone in it, so I can't verify that." Now, presumably when you testified in 1999, Mr. Duncan, your recollection of events in Central Bosnia was much fresher than it is today.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we consider the language that you used in that response when referring to the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Brigade, you mention "purported, apparently, whether this is fact or fiction." The truth is you didn't know for certain whether either the Mujahedin or the 7th Muslim Brigade existed, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: No, it's on the record. I mean, this is eight years ago for me, and if that's what I said, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the document that you were shown that was, interestingly enough, prepared by Colonel Guy Chambers at UNPROFOR, and this is the UNPROFOR BH Command at Kiseljak. You discussed Colonel Chambers a little earlier in your evidence, but the fact is he was a -- it was his role at Kiseljak to analyse and collate evidence -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, to analyse and collate information received from UNPROFOR units at a lower level; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, because he worked in the G2 cell, which was information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so to that extent, Colonel Chambers or Major Chambers, as he was then, was desk-bound, and he didn't go out himself to investigate and gather information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: He -- I would hope he would get out and have a look around, but he might not have done at all, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that his primary source of information about the Mujahedin was from Brit-Bat?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Well, he would have hopefully not used just one source but as many as he could find. It would have been foolish, I would have thought, to have just one source as you're putting out a message to somebody across the force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me when I say that the document that we saw doesn't really introduce any fresh source of information about the Mujahedin; when that report was prepared, Colonel Chambers was simply repeating information that he had been provided to him by others?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that's what he's done, yes, in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you, how much longer do you still have to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would anticipate about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've logged the same time now as the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, with the Court's indulgence, I would respectfully ask for a little more time, because obviously this is an important witness that touches upon crucial issues. I will try to be as quick as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a series of documents that show a different picture relating to command and control in Central Bosnia. We can start with document D270. While we're waiting, this is a milinfosum dated the 8th of May, 1993. At the top -- just under the heading, it states: "1. Vitez Area Cease-fire." If we can look at the bottom of the second paragraph, just above the part that says "a cessation of all hostilities," there's a comment prepared there, and I'm interested in the final sentence, and what it states is: "After initial mutual hostility, an agreement was reached even though both sides mentioned uncontrollable elements. "Comment: Command and control is often tenuous at best and elements of both factions operate outside of all authority. Comment ends." Now, Mr. Duncan, this was a generalised comment, but would you agree that this described problems found across the whole of the 3rd Corps' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: The first point -- am I allowed to point out this was -- we hadn't taken over at this stage as a regiment. We took over afterwards, I think on the 11th. And the main thrust of your comment was about the comment, and we've discussed that before, that the comments are not exact fact. So that comment about uncontrollable elements has been made by -- as a comment, and it's not a fact, unless I've got it horribly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can I clarify this, please, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you clarify, there's a little housekeeping matter. Now that you have asked for extra time, can we ask the witness who is waiting in the waiting room to go back to the hotel and be excused for the day. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can I just clarify your last answer?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've said that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We haven't actually taken over the regiment at that stage, I don't think. It's a minor problem, but it means that I'm not reading this as checking it through. And, secondly, you've pointed out about -- the bit about uncontrollable elements was a comment, and I thought that we discussed earlier that comments should be looked at with caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I entirely agree with you, Mr. Duncan, in respect of that last -- in respect of the last part of that answer, but if I could just clarify this. We see here a document which has "PWO Milinfosum" written on the top of it. Are you saying that somebody else produced this document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It's part of the takeover, hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I would remind you that at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, you told the Trial Chamber that the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment arrived on the 11th of April, 1993. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I've obviously mistimed my comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a second document, if I may. It's D271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What shall we do with D270?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I keep forgetting. I apologise. Please, could it be tendered for admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May it be given an exhibit number, please, and entered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 300 [Realtime transcript read in error "293"].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: While we're wait for this document, I'll explain that it's milinfosum number 20, dated the 19th of May, 1993. It's page 1 that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, sorry, if I may interrupt. Again, the record says "this is Exhibit 293", and I thought I heard you say "Exhibit 300", Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the record will please show it's 300 and not 293.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: First of all, concerning the date of this document, do you agree that the Prince of Wales' Own was firmly on the ground and operating by this time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just look towards the bottom, we don't have to move the screen, actually, it's the comment at the bottom that I'm interested in; although, the value of this may be in question, but taking into account what you've just told us, what it says is that: "Certain individuals are beyond the control of all recognised authority has been apparent for some time. Whether because it is a convenient excuse for noncompliance or not, uncontrollable elements are constantly referred to in the meetings of the joint commissions for all areas. The concern is that their actions will incite others." Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I have, that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it's correct to say, isn't it, that at the 19th of May, 1993, ARBiH commanders in different areas were telling Brit-Bat repeatedly that there were elements beyond their control; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Everybody was reporting elements beyond their control. It's not just ABiH or HVO, it's everybody's reporting this, and it's a comment, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender that document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 301.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to refer to is D273, and it's milinfosum number 29, dated 28 May 1993, and it's page 1 that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we can see there, point number 2 is headed "Travnik," and I'm interested in point number 4, which is lower down the page. What we can see here is that it states: "This afternoon the Travnik LO," that's "liaison officer," "... reported that Leutar and Alagic had told him that they were losing control of their respective commands and, therefore, the situation as a whole." Now, would you agree with me that around the 28th of May, the system of command and control was breaking down in the area of responsibility of General Alagic, i.e., the OG Bosanska Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: We're talking about Travnik at this stage, and the relationship between the HVO and BiH in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes. And as it says here, because of that situation, we deployed additional people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So command and control was breaking down in Travnik around the 28th of May; you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, I would admit that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, if we could admit this document into evidence, please, or tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the issue of control over the Mujahedin, and in this respect if we can refer to Exhibit D274. This is milinfosum number 32. It's dated the 31st of May, 1993, and it's the first page that we're interested in. If we could scroll down the page, please, to the Zenica section. That's fine. If I could read this extract to you, it states: "The Zenica LO today attended a meeting with the Mujahedin elements based in Zenica. He spoke with three representatives, all from Turkey, with only one able to speak Serbo-Croat. They were friendly but guarded when asked questions of a military nature, such as their relations with the mainstream BiH. They were very suspicious of the activities of both UNPROFOR and the UNHCR. The LO formed the impression that they regarded the Croats as a bigger enemy than the Serbs and that they were not under control of 3rd Corps." Now it's right, Mr. Duncan, isn't it, that the liaison officer who provided this information and concluded that those Mujahedin were not under the control of the 3rd Corps, had actually met those men and talked with them?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that's something that you never did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. Have you considered they could be under the headquarters above the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, it's not my role to question the evidence. I'll leave that for the skills of the Judges. But what I'm interested in is that this report is dated the 31st of May and comes some four days after another milinfosum that the Prosecutor showed you, which indicated that the Mujahedin in Zenica were under the control of the 3rd Corps, and to come back to what you said about five minutes ago, perhaps could this have been a situation where the liaison officer had gone back to try and clarify the situation or investigate?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: It could well have done, yes, because when he brought the information in, it would have to be verified if we've got another source against a single source. So we'd try and find out more information, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if indeed he verified, the conclusion is clear here, isn't it, that the Mujahedin were not under control of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: As it stands, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please could I tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 303.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd now like to turn to document D275, but I'm conscious that it's -- I think it was admitted as an exhibit earlier, but perhaps if we can bring up 275, and we can identify the exhibit number, if indeed that's the case, just to explain that this is another milinfosum, number 45, dated the 13th of June, 1993. It's the first page we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So Mr. Duncan, if I can just touch upon what the first paragraph says. At the bottom, the last sentence of the first paragraph, it says: "ACs conducted an extensive recce of the area and noted the following detail:" And if we look at point B it says that: "The village of Guca Gora is occupied by Mujahedin elements in some strength, 25 to 30 observed the group contained Arabic speakers and refused to talk via a female interpreter. Some of the group were clearly hostile to the UN. When asked about the cease-fire, they denied all knowledge, and when shown a copy, they claimed that it did not apply to them." First of all, by "cease-fire," this would have been an agreement between the HVO and Bosnian Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, according to this statement, the fact that the Mujahedin elements stated that they did not consider themselves to be bound by such agreements, would you agree that that provides a clear indication that they were not under the control of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN.
utterances.text: That's what they've said, that they're not under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That was the information reported back to Brit-Bat headquarters that day. Your Honour, I'm told that that was Exhibit 287. Your Honour, I do have only a small number of exhibits, not many at all, but I did receive a letter -- a note informing me that the Prosecutor had some matters to raise, so -- and perhaps this might be an appropriate moment for my learned friend to interject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have issues to raise before we break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I had just a couple of very brief issues before we break. I'm assuming that Mr. Robson needs some time tomorrow morning. I would ask that I be given just a couple of minutes before we -- before we break. If it's clear that he's going into tomorrow, then I would need a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would say is that I've probably got no more than 15 minutes worth of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll have to go into tomorrow, then. Let's give Mr. Mundis an opportunity. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that we go into private session. There's no need, actually, for the witness to remain. He can be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that. Mr. Duncan, we are about to knock off in another four minutes' time, and apparently there are other issues to attend to. You are excused for the day, but please come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in this courtroom, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask we go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that we are in open session, we can adjourn to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
